Homoiousios
hoh-moy-OO-see-os
n./adj. (Greek; historical theology; fourth-century Christology)
From Greek homoios (similar, like, resembling; distinct from homos, same, identical) + ousia (substance, essence, being); the compound means “of similar substance.” Contrasts with homoousios (“of the same substance,” the Nicene confession) and heteroousios (“of different substance,” the strict Arian position). The prefix difference of one letter — homoi- vs. homo- — is the grammatical marker of the entire Nicene controversy.

Biblical Definition

Homoiousios (Greek: ὁμοιούσιος, “of similar substance”) is the fourth-century semi-Arian term for the relationship between the Father and the Son, distinguishing it from the orthodox homoousios (“of the same substance”) by the single letter iota. The Nicene Creed (AD 325) had declared the Son to be homoousios with the Father — of identical divine substance. The semi-Arians proposed homoiousios as a mediating position: the Son is “of similar substance” to the Father, alike in quality but not identical in essence. The difference is not pedantic: homoousios affirms the full identity of divine nature between Father and Son; homoiousios makes the Son a subordinate divine being of analogous but distinct substance. Athanasius of Alexandria rightly recognized that homoiousios preserved Arianism's essential subordinationism under a more palatable formula. John's Gospel brooks no ambiguity: “In the beginning, the Word already was — face-to-face with God, and Himself God” (John 1:1); “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” (Col 2:9). Hebrews 1:3 adds: He is “the exact representation of His nature.” If the Son is only similar to the Father, He is less than the Father, and the entire edifice of Christian salvation collapses — for only one who is truly and fully God can reconcile humanity to God. The iota between homoousios and homoiousios is the line between the God who saves and a demigod who cannot.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fourth-century semi-Arian term for the Son as “of similar substance” to the Father — the mediating but theologically fatal alternative to the Nicene homoousios, preserving Arianism's essential subordinationism under a more plausible and irenic formula.

HOMOIOUSIOS, adj./n. (Greek ὁμοιούσιος). “Of similar substance”; the semi-Arian formula proposed in the fourth-century Trinitarian controversy as a middle way between strict Arianism (heteroousios: “of different substance”) and Nicene orthodoxy (homoousios: “of the same substance”).

The single letter difference — homoios (similar) vs. homos (same) — carries the weight of the entire Nicene controversy. Athanasius held, rightly, that homoiousios ultimately conceded Arian subordinationism: a Son who is merely similar to the Father is a secondary divine being, not the one God of Israel in the second Person.

The homoiousian party (Basil of Ancyra, George of Laodicea) represented a sincere anti-Arian conservatism that resisted the mechanical Arianism of Eusebius of Nicomedia but was unwilling to commit to homoousios, which they feared could imply Sabellian modalism. Jerome famously quipped that the whole world “groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian” during the years of semi-Arian imperial dominance (356–381 AD).

The Council of Constantinople (381 AD) reaffirmed homoousios and expanded the Creed to articulate the Spirit's full divinity, settling the Trinitarian question in favor of Nicene orthodoxy and against all gradations of homoiousios or Arian subordinationism.

Neo-Arian movements today — Jehovah's Witnesses, Oneness Pentecostalism, and various liberal theologies reducing the Son to the “highest expression of God” — functionally recapitulate homoiousios even without the vocabulary. The test question remains Athanasius's: Is the Son of identical divine substance with the Father, or is He something less?

Key Scripture

John 10:30 — "I and my Father are one."

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Hebrews 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;"

Modern Corruption

The homoiousios formula is the corruption — a fourth-century attempt to preserve Arian subordinationism under softer language; modern neo-Arian movements in cults and liberal theology recapitulate it by making the Son a secondary divine being.

expand to see more

The historical homoiousian position was not malicious compromise but sincere theological confusion. The semi-Arians feared that homoousios (one substance) implied Sabellian modalism — that Father and Son were merely two modes of one Person. But Athanasius and the Cappadocian Fathers (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa) demonstrated that homoousios is compatible with a robust distinction of Persons: one essence (ousia), three Persons (hypostaseis). The solution was not homoiousios but a more precise vocabulary of Person and substance. The lesson is that doctrinal imprecision adopted to avoid one error often enables another.

Jehovah's Witnesses, Mormonism, and Oneness Pentecostalism each deny the Nicene homoousios in different ways but with the common effect of making the Son something less than the one God. Jehovah's Witnesses render John 1:1 as “the Word was a god” (New World Translation) to achieve a homoiousios-equivalent result without the Greek vocabulary. The Reformed pastor's task is not merely to cite the Creed but to walk through the exegesis: if the Son is not homoousios with the Father, He cannot be the LORD of Isaiah 6:1 whom John declares He is (John 12:41), He cannot bear the divine Name above every name (Phil 2:9-11), and the atoning work cannot reconcile humanity to God because only God Himself is equal to the task.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Greek homoios (similar) + ousia (substance, essence); the contrast with homoousios (homos + ousia, same substance) turns on the prefix, producing a theological gulf from a grammatical hairsbreadth.

expand to see more

Greek homoios (ὅμοιος) — similar, like, resembling; distinct from homos (same, identical); the prefix homo- in homoousios means same; the prefix homoi- in homoiousios means merely similar — one vowel shift, one universe of theological difference.

Greek ousia (οὐσία) — substance, essence, being; in Platonic and Aristotelian usage, the essential nature of a thing; in Trinitarian theology, the one divine essence shared (homoousios) or analogized (homoiousios) between Father and Son.

Greek hypostasis (ὑπόστασις) — person, underlying reality, subsistence; the Cappadocian solution was mia ousia, treis hypostaseis (one essence, three Persons), distinguishing the shared nature from the distinct Persons and answering the semi-Arian fear of modalism without retreating to homoiousios.

Greek heteroousios (ἑτεροούσιος) — of different substance; the strict Arian position (Arius, Eunomius) that the Son is of a completely different substance from the Father, a first and greatest creature; homoiousios occupied the middle ground between this and Nicene orthodoxy.

Latin consubstantialis — consubstantial, of the same substance; the Latin West's rendering of homoousios; the Nicene Creed in English now translates it as “consubstantial with the Father,” a rendering that restores the technical precision that “of one Being” had softened.

Usage

"The homoiousios controversy is a pastoral case study in how theological imprecision enables doctrinal collapse by degrees: one iota of difference was the difference between the triune God of salvation and a high divine creature who cannot save."

"When a congregation begins describing the Son as “the most God-like being” or “perfectly reflecting the Father” without affirming full homoousios identity, the slide toward functional homoiousios has begun — a slide that eventually collapses the atonement."

"The Nicene resolution remains the test of orthodoxy: confessing the Son as “consubstantial with the Father” is not fourth-century Greek philosophy imported into Christianity but the biblical insistence that the One who redeems is the One who created — the LORD Himself come in the flesh."
